name: JarvX
tagline: A Jarvis-style AI assistant you summon on your desktop instead of opening a chat tab.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The hard part of a personal AI assistant is not the intelligence, it is the plumbing: a global hotkey, a floating window that does not steal focus badly, context from whatever you are looking at, and a model call that streams fast enough to feel instant. An agent can wire all of that in a sitting if you accept a single desktop platform and your own API key. What you will not get in one shot is the polish layer: codesigned builds, auto-update, permission prompts that do not scare people, and a mobile companion. If the product's real pitch is deep OS automation or a tuned agent loop over your apps, the gap widens from a weekend to a project. Confidence here is low because this is a small product and the feature surface is not something to assume.
coreLoopDIY: A hotkey-summoned floating window that sends your prompt plus the current clipboard or selected text to an LLM and streams the answer back, with local history.
requirements: An LLM API key, OpenAI or Anthropic, billed per token
macOS or Windows, pick one, accessibility and clipboard permissions
Comfort with an unsigned local build, or paying for a code signing certificate
whatYouLose: Signed, auto-updating builds that your OS does not warn you about
Prebuilt app and OS integrations someone else already debugged
Latency and prompt tuning that was done for you
A support channel when the hotkey stops firing after an OS update
moatNotes: Desktop assistants live and die on feel: summon speed, focus handling, and not breaking on OS updates. None of that is conceptually hard, all of it is tedious.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because an assistant you have to babysit is not an assistant. Paying means someone else owns the codesigning, the permission dialogs, the OS update that silently kills global hotkeys, and the model routing that keeps responses snappy. A self-built version works great for a month and then quietly stops launching, and at that point your free tool costs you an evening of debugging instead of a few dollars.
notes: The chat part is trivial now; the hotkey-and-permissions part is where weekends go to die.
prompt:
Build a desktop AI assistant for macOS that I run locally. Stack: Tauri 2 with React and TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind. No accounts, no telemetry, no cloud backend.

Core behavior:
- A global hotkey, Cmd+Shift+Space, toggles a small always-on-top, frameless, transparent-background window centered near the top of the screen. Pressing Escape hides it. The window must not take over the dock or app switcher.
- The window is a single text input plus a streamed response area. Enter sends, Shift+Enter makes a newline.
- On summon, capture the current clipboard text and show it as a dismissible context chip. If the user keeps it, prepend it to the prompt as context.
- Stream responses from the Anthropic Messages API using a key from .env as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Read it in the Rust side, never ship it to the renderer.
- Keep conversation turns in memory for the current session. Cmd+K starts a fresh session.
- Persist every session to a local SQLite file in the app data directory. Add a history view reachable with Cmd+H: list sessions by date, click to reopen read-only, with a delete button.
- Copy button on each response that writes to the clipboard.

Explicitly out of scope: login, sync, mobile, file uploads, voice input, tool use or app automation, auto-update, analytics.

Deliverables: working dev build via npm run tauri dev, a .env.example, and a README covering the hotkey, where the SQLite file lives, how to change the model name in one place, and the macOS accessibility permission you have to grant on first run. Keep the UI quiet: dark, one accent color, no splash screen, no onboarding.
